newsitem.title: VIETNAM: FEATURE-Vietnam faces possible hard toil in Year of Ox.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Vietnam faces possible hard toil in Year of Ox.

text.p: Vietnam celebrates its biggest annual festival, the Tet Lunar New Year, this week while facing one of its most uncertain periods in years.
As the old year draws to a close, crowds throng the markets in Hanoi's oldest quarters where local merchants tap the holiday spirit with sales of cherry blossom and Kumquat citrus trees.

But despite the festive activity, not all is well 10 years down Hanoi's economic reforms path as the country's 77 million people prepare for the Year of the Ox -- traditionally characterised as an animal of hard toil.
"I'm having to sell at very low prices," said a market trader. "I'm losing a lot of money, but I don't know what else to do. Tet is coming."
The uncharacteristically downcast mood at this auspicious time is reflected in many areas. Some people blame the weather while others cite a range of factors.
The communist government has announced tough steps in recent weeks aimed at tackling problems of insidious graft, consumerism, crime, drugs and declining traditional morals.
The state has splashed lurid details of major corruption cases across the media, while rhetoric reminiscent of the pre-reform era has appeared in government-approved commentaries.
Together with a catalogue of apparently restrictive decrees and regulations this has prompted warnings that Vietnam is bracing for tighter state controls.

"I saw that said in one (foreign) paper, and if I was the government I'd be mad about statements like that," said one long-term foreign resident. "Sure the leadership wants control, but what government doesn't?"
FOREIGN BUSINESSES SCALING BACK
But after more than a year of fiery propaganda, leadership tussles, business failings, media clampdowns and tough government campaigns, it is easy to believe the worst.

Economic fundamentals remain good -- a large potential market, strong growth, high productivity and lowish inflation -- but that is cold comfort for resident foreign executives facing evaporating boardroom interest in Vietnam back at head office.

"Vietnam's not been a great career decision," said an executive. "Right now we're only that far from scaling everything back, flying in some old hand who can do no harm and pulling everyone else out."
Political analysts said the mood reflected factionalism at the top levels in Vietnam.
"I think what we're seeing is a gradual sidelining of the reformers," said a prominent Western Vietnam watcher.
"I don't think there's any indication of a government close to collapse, but if this continues it's likely to play into the hands of an increasingly authoritarian regime."
LEADERSHIP SEEN MAKING ATTEMPT TO BOOST MORALE
Whichever way one reads the tea leaves, Vietnam's traditionally closed leadership seems to want to brighten the mood ahead of the new year.

With just days to go before the Tet celebrations Hanoi performed a Lazarus act with the surprise appearance on television of its head of state, President Le Duc Anh, 10 weeks after suffering a stroke and disappearing from public view.
Officials at state broadcaster VTV said Anh -- a member of the elite ruling triumvirate -- was likely to deliver a rallying call to the nation in a telecast to mark the Tet.
In addition, Communist Party Secretary General Do Muoi was expected to be filmed marking the new year's arrival by beating a traditional bronze drum.
"They want to do something to restore people's enthusiasm," said one Hanoi office worker.
